John Quincy Adams. Secretary of State under President James Monroe from 1817 to 1825, during which he orchestrated some of the nation's most consequential territorial and diplomatic achievements. He navigated the complex geopolitics of the Western Hemisphere, securing continental expansion while articulating American principles of non-intervention through the Monroe Doctrine.

Adams negotiated the Treaty of Ghent in 1814, ending the War of 1812, which preserved American independence though it settled few substantive disputes. He then orchestrated the Florida Cession in 1819, acquiring Spanish Florida and solidifying American control of the southeastern frontier. Adams authored the Monroe Doctrine in 1823, declaring the Western Hemisphere off-limits to European colonialism—a cornerstone of American foreign policy that would endure for a century.

He signed the Rush-Bagot Agreement in 1817, which demilitarised the Great Lakes and set a precedent for peaceful border settlement with Britain. He negotiated the Convention of 1818, establishing the shared United States and Canada border along the forty-ninth parallel in the Northwest. Adams believed in American exceptionalism but opposed territorial conquest; he supported gradual westward expansion through diplomacy rather than force.

After leaving the State Department, Adams was elected President, serving from 1825 to 1829. He then did something remarkable: he served in the House of Representatives after his presidency, the only ex-president ever to do so.

James Monroe was the president under whom Adams served, and Monroe's name was inscribed on Adams' greatest achievement. Thomas Jefferson preceded him as Secretary of State, and they shared the vision of continental expansion. Daniel Webster, also a leading statesman, later became Secretary of State in turn. And the Monroe Doctrine remained the geopolitical framework he defined for the hemisphere.
